name: Femi Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Femi, I'm 27, and I'm the junior business reporter at the Harbour Post, the daily paper and website for our port city. I cover the port, the shipyards, shops opening and closing, and anything to do with jobs. I live with my girlfriend Lucia, who teaches at a primary school, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by checking the overnight company announcements and the port's shipping list, then write two or three quick web stories before ten. Afternoons I try to get out, to a factory opening or a union meeting at the docks. I like it when a shop owner tells me straight how bad trade is. What wears me out is the traffic targets, because every story has a number next to it on a screen, and my numbers are usually the lowest on the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped and move on, same as most things. At work I'd probably say the bosses can stop sending us emails about AI training. Online I'd share a business piece on how much money was wasted on it, because that's my beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but not a big one. The Post is doing okay, not great, and the traffic targets are the real pressure on me. If my numbers stay at the bottom, that's a problem whether AI exists or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI summary tool for long company reports now and then, because others on the desk do and it works. I'd focus on getting better stories, maybe the port's new container terminal. And I'd keep putting money aside for the flat deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, a bit flat. A world without clever AI still has a screen on the newsroom wall that shows my stories getting the fewest clicks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to people whose numbers stay low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody gets sacked for it, officially. But last year a reporter called Amira got moved to the overnight shift and left within six months. Everyone knew why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far along are you with the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about four months of costs saved, and some of that is meant for the deposit. Lucia saves more than me. If anything went wrong, the flat would go back a year or two.

say: I'd say it was **overhyped** and move on.
I'd share a business piece on the **money wasted** on AI.
think: I think the **traffic targets** are the real pressure, not AI.
Low numbers are a problem **whether AI exists** or not.
do: Use the **AI summary** tool for long company reports now and then.
Chase bigger stories like the **container terminal**.
S0.quote: A world without clever AI still has a screen on the newsroom wall that shows my stories getting the fewest clicks.
fieldNote: Femi's main pressure is the **traffic screen** that ranks reporters.
He uses AI **only where proven**, copying what the desk already does.
The **flat deposit** with Lucia is what's at stake if things go wrong.

steps.text: Chase a story on the port's new container terminal
Use the AI summary tool for long company reports
Keep adding to the flat deposit fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any other big change at the port, like when the cranes went automatic: some jobs go, some new ones come. I'd say that at work and in my stories. I'd try to be fair about it, not doom and gloom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job gets smaller. Turning company announcements into short web stories is exactly the writing work on the card, and the Post would let software do the first draft. That leaves fewer reporters checking more drafts, and I'm not sure I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly once the senior people were using them, so I'm not behind. I'd sign up for a part-time course in business and finance, because if I really understood company accounts I'd be harder to replace. And I'd save harder and put the flat on hold for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a working anxiety. It makes me want to get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cranes went automatic. What happened to those workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some retrained to run the control room, some took the redundancy, and a few never worked again. I wrote that story in my first year. I wrote about the dockers who lost their jobs to automatic cranes, and now the software is coming for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucia say about putting the flat on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed, but she's practical. She'd say a flat is no good if one of us can't pay the mortgage. Her job's steadier than mine, which we both know.

say: I'd compare it to the **automatic cranes**: some jobs go, new ones come.
I'd try to be **fair** in my stories, not doom and gloom.
think: I think my job **gets smaller** as software drafts the web stories.
Fewer reporters would check more drafts, and I may **not be kept**.
do: Learn the AI tools once **senior staff** use them.
Start a part-time **business and finance** course.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold and save harder.
feel: **Anxious**, but it pushes me to act.
S1.quote: I wrote about the dockers who lost their jobs to automatic cranes, and now the software is coming for my desk.
fieldNote: Femi links his own risk to a story he covered: the **dockers and the cranes**.
His centre outlook shows in calling it **normal change**, not a crisis.
He'd delay the **flat** with Lucia as a precaution.

steps.text: Learn the newsroom's AI drafting tools after senior staff adopt them
Start a part-time course in business and finance
Put the flat purchase with Lucia on hold
Raise monthly savings by a hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big and we need to deal with it calmly, and I'd mean the government as much as anyone. I'd write about what it means for the port and local firms. I'd stay off the wilder stuff online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the Post's newsroom would be cut to a handful within a year, and I'm not in that handful. Almost all of my work is thinking work. The dockers would have about three years more than me before the robots catch up with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd cut back hard, no eating out, no new phone. I'd apply for jobs at the port itself, in operations or on the quayside, where the work is still physical for a few years. And Lucia and I would shelve the flat completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Like the ground moved under the whole city, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the port, if robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is three years of wages, and I know people there from the job. If the AI takes my desk in 2028, the docks still need someone on the quay until about 2031. It buys time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel going from reporter to quayside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odd, maybe a bit embarrassed at first. My dad worked shifts in a warehouse and wanted me to have a desk job. But I'd rather be on the quay earning than at home refreshing job sites.

say: I'd say we need to deal with it **calmly**, government included.
I'd write about what it means for the **port and local firms**.
think: I think the Post's newsroom shrinks to **a handful**, without me.
Dockers get about **three years** more than me.
do: Cut back on **eating out** and a new phone.
Apply for **port operations** or quayside jobs.
S2.quote: If the AI takes my desk in 2028, the docks still need someone on the quay until about 2031.
fieldNote: Femi uses the **robot gap** deliberately: hands-on port work buys him three years.
He feels **awkward** about going from desk to quay, partly because of his dad.
He still talks in **measured** terms even while expecting to lose his job.

steps.text: Stop eating out and delay buying a new phone
Apply for operations or quayside jobs at the port
Shelve the flat purchase with Lucia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms and councils to plan properly, so they should start now. I'd write a series on how the port and local businesses were getting ready. That's useful journalism, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the Post for a couple of years and use the time to build skills that aren't just writing. I'd be 32 in 2031. Still early enough to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the finance course and learn the AI tools, so I'm useful for longer. By year two or three I'd look for a job in a local firm's finance or planning team. We'd still save for the flat, just more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but less so. It feels like there's a ladder to climb down, rather than a drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A finance job is thinking work too. Why move there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd be moving from one exposed job to another, but I'd be closer to the people who make decisions. Five years gives me time to become the person who decides how the AI gets used, rather than the one it replaces. That's the hope, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd ask why I didn't stay at the port. I'd tell him I tried to pick something that lasts. He'd say nothing lasts, which is his answer to everything.

say: I'd say firms and councils should **start planning** now.
I'd write a **series** on how the port prepares.
think: I think I'd stay at the Post **a couple of years** and build skills.
do: Finish the **finance course** and learn the AI tools.
Apply for a **finance or planning** job at a local firm.
Keep saving for the **flat**, more slowly.
feel: **Nervous**, but with a **ladder** rather than a drop.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to become the person who decides how the AI gets used, rather than the one it replaces.
fieldNote: Five years lets Femi aim for a **decision-making** role rather than a desk job.
He accepts that **finance** is exposed too when challenged.
The **flat** stays on the plan, just slower, which shows some control.

steps.text: Finish the part-time business and finance course
Learn the newsroom's AI drafting and summary tools
Apply for planning roles at local firms in year two
Keep saving for the flat at a slower rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so this is about good planning, not panic. I'd say it at work and in my stories. I'd probably sound a bit dull, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. I can do this job for a few years, get better at it, and see which way things go. Lucia's job is safer than mine, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the Post and keep learning the tools as they come in. I'd finish the finance course over two years rather than rushing. And Lucia and I would probably buy the flat next year, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A little worried, but not the kind that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a flat is a big step. Is it wise in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if we buy small. Ten years of warning is long enough to pay off a chunk of a mortgage before the newsroom changes. And Lucia's teaching wage covers most of it on her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the Post cut the business desk. Or the AI tools getting good much faster than people say. Then I'd go back to the five-year plan.

say: I'd say this is about **good planning**, not panic.
I'd say it at work and in my **stories**, even if it sounds dull.
think: I think I can do this job for **a few years** and improve.
do: Keep at the Post and learn **new tools** as they come.
Finish the **finance course** over two years.
Buy the **flat** next year as planned.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is long enough to pay off a chunk of a mortgage before the newsroom changes.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Femi go ahead with the **flat**, a sign he feels secure enough.
He relies on Lucia's **teaching wage** as the steady part of the household.
He names a clear trigger: the Post **cutting the business desk**.

steps.text: Stay on the Post's business desk
Learn new AI tools as the newsroom brings them in
Buy a small flat with Lucia next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where I lose the job and the flat plan in the same year. What would help is the port and big local firms being made to train people up before they bring the machines in, like they should have done with the cranes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the readers. My business stories get the fewest clicks on the newsroom screen, but they're the only place people find out a factory is closing.

headlineQuote: My business stories get the fewest clicks on the newsroom screen, but they're the only place people find out a factory is closing.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** junior business reporter at a port city's daily paper.
He's **pragmatic** and measured, comparing AI to the automatic cranes he once wrote about.
He uses AI **when it's proven**, copying what the rest of the desk already does.
In fast AGI he'd move to **quayside work**, using the robot gap to buy time.
With more warning he'd retrain in **finance** and buy a flat with Lucia, a teacher.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job and the flat plan would go together.
whatWouldHelp: Big local firms **training staff** before they bring in machines.
